title: Bonding as a continuum: the bonding triangle
html:
Guiding question

How do the models of bonding and structure help us to design new materials?

Do now: what is the difference between ionic, covalent and metallic bonding? How do we know which type of bonding a material has, and what if a material shows properties of two types?

So far you have met three bonding models: ionic (S2.1), covalent (S2.2) and metallic (S2.3). Real substances rarely fit one model perfectly. This topic treats bonding as a continuum and uses it to explain and design materials: alloys, addition polymers and (AHL) condensation polymers.

S2.4.1 Bonding is a continuum: the bonding triangle

Bonds can be thought of as:

  • ionic: electrons fully transferred from one atom to another (large difference in electronegativity);
  • covalent: electron pairs shared equally (both atoms have high electronegativity, small difference);
  • polar covalent: electron pairs shared unequally (intermediate difference);
  • metallic: valence electrons delocalized (both atoms have low electronegativity, small difference).

The difference in electronegativity between the two atoms is the first clue to which type of bonding is likely. But one number is not enough: Cs and F₂ both have Δχ = 0, yet one is a metal and the other a covalent molecule. We also need to know how high the electronegativities are.

"Pure" ionic and "pure" covalent bonds are idealized models. Most real bonds sit somewhere between the three types. The van Arkel–Ketelaar triangle (bonding triangle, in the data booklet) shows this two-dimensional continuum using two electronegativity values.

Difference in electronegativity (y-axis): Δχ = χlarger − χsmaller
Average electronegativity (x-axis): Σχ = (χA + χB) / 2
  • Top corner: ionic (large Δχ, e.g. CsF).
  • Bottom left: metallic (low average χ, small Δχ, e.g. Cs, Na).
  • Bottom right: covalent (high average χ, small Δχ, e.g. F₂, Cl₂).
  • Regions in between: polar covalent and semi-metallic (metalloid) bonding, e.g. Si, B.

The triangle was developed by Anton Eduard van Arkel and J. A. A. Ketelaar. Its message is that bond types are connected: compounds have varying degrees of each kind of bonding character, and "polar covalent" is simply a region of the continuum between covalent and ionic.

Electronegativity values (Pauling scale) come from the data booklet. The triangle also has a percentage ionic character scale along the y-axis.

Common mistakeThe x-axis is the average (mean) electronegativity, not the sum, even though it is sometimes labelled Σχ. Divide by 2. For an element (e.g. Cl₂ or Na), Δχ = 0 and the average equals the electronegativity of the element.

Which corner of the bonding triangle corresponds to a low average electronegativity and a small Δχ?

  1. Ionic (top)
  2. Covalent (bottom right)
  3. Metallic (bottom left)
  4. Polar covalent (middle)

Both atoms hold their electrons weakly (low χ) and equally (small Δχ), so the valence electrons delocalize: metallic bonding. Small Δχ with high χ is covalent.

Locating substances on the triangle

Method: (1) look up both electronegativities in the data booklet; (2) Δχ = large − small (y-axis); (3) average = sum ÷ 2 (x-axis); (4) plot the point and read the region.

Worked example

Use χ(Na) = 0.9, χ(H) = 2.2, χ(Cl) = 3.2.

SubstanceΔχ (y)Average χ (x)Region
Cl₂3.2 − 3.2 = 0(3.2 + 3.2)/2 = 3.2Covalent
HCl3.2 − 2.2 = 1.0(3.2 + 2.2)/2 = 2.7Polar covalent
NaCl3.2 − 0.9 = 2.3(3.2 + 0.9)/2 = 2.05Ionic
Na00.9Metallic

Read the point off the triangle: find the average on the x-axis, then go up to the Δχ value and see which region the point falls in.

Common mistakeFor NaCl, use χ(Cl) = 3.2, not the value for hydrogen (2.2). It is easy to copy the wrong number from the HCl line: Δχ for NaCl is 2.3 and the average is 2.05.

Calculate Δχ for magnesium oxide. χ(Mg) = 1.3, χ(O) = 3.4.

Δχ = 3.4 − 1.3 = 2.1. The average is (3.4 + 1.3)/2 = 2.35, which places MgO in the ionic region.
Worked example

Question: Estimate the percentage ionic character of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃. χ(Al) = 1.6, χ(O) = 3.4.

  1. Δχ = 3.4 − 1.6 = 1.8
  2. Average χ = (3.4 + 1.6)/2 = 2.5
  3. Plotting (2.5, 1.8) on the triangle gives a point just inside the ionic region, about 55–60 % ionic character. Al₂O₃ is mostly ionic but has significant covalent character, which is consistent with it being amphoteric.
Exam question: locate (a) phosphorus, (b) caesium iodide and (c) brass on the triangle. Work out the coordinates first, then reveal

Other useful examples: CsI (large Δχ, low average) is ionic. Phosphorus (Δχ = 0, average 2.2) is covalent, near the metalloid border. Brass (Cu 1.9, Zn 1.6: Δχ = 0.3, average ≈ 1.75) is metallic.

For CsI: χ(Cs) = 0.8, χ(I) = 2.7, so Δχ = 1.9 and average = 1.75: in the ionic region.

Calculate the average electronegativity (x-axis value) for HCl. χ(H) = 2.2, χ(Cl) = 3.2.

(2.2 + 3.2) / 2 = 2.7. With Δχ = 1.0, HCl falls in the polar covalent region.
Key pointA single bond type is a model. The bonding triangle shows that substances have varying degrees of ionic, covalent and metallic character. For example, AlCl₃ has a Δχ of 1.6 but behaves largely as a covalent (molecular) compound, because the small, highly charged Al³⁺ ion distorts (polarizes) the electron cloud of Cl⁻.

title: Bonding, structure and properties
html:
S2.4.2 Bonding, structure and properties

Once you know the bonding and structure, you can predict physical properties: melting point, volatility, electrical conductivity, solubility and hardness. You can also work backwards from properties to bonding.

Four types of structure

  • Giant ionic: crystalline structures in which ions are held together by electrostatic attraction (ionic bonds). No intermolecular forces.
  • Giant covalent (macromolecular): crystalline structures in which atoms are held together by strong covalent bonds throughout. No intermolecular forces.
  • Simple covalent (molecular): separate molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces; the covalent bonds inside each molecule are strong.
  • Giant metallic: crystalline structures in which metal cations are held together by a sea of delocalized electrons. No intermolecular forces.
StructureParticles and forcesMelting pointConducts as solid?Conducts as liquid?Conducts in aqueous solution?Solubility in water
Giant ionic (e.g. NaCl, Tm 801 °C)Ions; strong electrostatic attraction in all directionsHighNo (ions fixed)Yes (mobile ions)YesOften soluble
Giant metallic (e.g. Mg, Tm 650 °C)Cations and delocalized electronsUsually highYesYesn/a (insoluble; some react)Insoluble
Giant covalent (e.g. diamond, SiO₂)Atoms; strong covalent bonds throughoutVery highNo (except graphite)Non/aInsoluble
Simple molecular (e.g. I₂ Tm 114 °C, ice 0 °C)Molecules; strong covalent bonds within, weak intermolecular forces betweenLowNoNoUsually no (some, e.g. HCl, ionize)Polar ones soluble; non-polar ones insoluble
Common mistakeGiant structures (ionic, metallic, giant covalent) have no intermolecular forces, because there are no molecules. Melting them means overcoming ionic bonds, metallic bonds or covalent bonds. Only simple molecular substances melt by overcoming intermolecular forces.

A solid has a melting point of 1450 °C. It does not conduct as a solid but conducts when molten. What is its structure?

  1. Giant covalent
  2. Giant ionic
  3. Giant metallic
  4. Simple molecular

High melting point plus conduction only when molten means the charge carriers are ions that are fixed in the solid and mobile in the liquid. A metal would also conduct as a solid; a giant covalent solid would not conduct at all.

Exam tipTo identify a giant covalent substance from data, look for a very high melting point, low solubility in water and no conductivity even when molten. A high melting point that conducts when molten but not as a solid points to ionic. One that conducts as a solid and as a liquid points to metallic.

Graphite is the exception among giant covalent structures. Each carbon uses three electrons in covalent bonds within a hexagonal layer, and the fourth electron is delocalized across the layer, so graphite conducts along the layers. Weak forces between the layers let them slide, which is why graphite is soft (used in pencils and as electrodes).

Which substance has the lowest melting point?

  1. Magnesium
  2. Sodium chloride
  3. Silicon dioxide
  4. Iodine

Iodine is simple molecular: melting overcomes only London forces between I₂ molecules (Tm 114 °C). The others are giant structures in which strong bonds must be broken.

Task: fill in a summary table (bonding or IMF, melting point, conductivity as solid / liquid / aqueous) for the four structure types. Then reveal the answers
StructureBonding or IMF overcome on meltingTmSolidLiquidAqueous
Giant covalentCovalent bonds (no IMF)HighNoNoNo (insoluble)
Giant ionic latticeIonic bonds (no IMF)Very highNoYesYes
Simple molecularIntermolecular forces (type depends on the molecule)LowNoNoNo (usually)
MetallicMetallic bonds (no IMF)HighYesYesn/a

title: Alloys
html:
S2.4.3 Alloys

Do now: what is bronze? What is rose gold? Why might we melt two different metals together?

DefinitionAn alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually other metals, sometimes non-metals such as carbon), with metallic bonding throughout. Alloys are made by mixing the molten components and letting them cool.

Metals do not react with each other to form compounds; instead they dissolve in one another to give a solid solution. Common examples are steel, brass, bronze and pewter.

Because metallic bonding is non-directional, a metal lattice can take in atoms of a different element without breaking the bonding. Metals with similar atomic radii and similar electronegativity mix especially well, which is why many transition metals alloy readily with one another.

Types of alloy

  • Substitutional alloy: atoms of the added metal replace some host atoms in the lattice. The atoms are of similar size (e.g. brass: Zn replaces some Cu; bronze: Sn in Cu).
  • Interstitial alloy: much smaller atoms fit into the gaps (interstices) between the host atoms (e.g. carbon in iron to make steel). The small atoms are usually non-metals such as C, N or H, rather than other metals.

Steel contains small carbon atoms in the gaps of the iron lattice. What type of alloy is this?

  1. Interstitial
  2. Substitutional
  3. Ionic
  4. Compound

Carbon atoms are much smaller than iron atoms, so they sit in the interstices (holes) of the lattice rather than replacing iron atoms.

Why alloys are harder and stronger than pure metals

In a pure metal, all the cations are the same size and are arranged in regular layers that slide easily. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes distort the regular lattice. The layers can no longer slide over one another easily, so a greater force is needed to deform the metal. The alloy is harder, stronger and less malleable than the pure metal (it has greater tensile strength).

Alloying makes a metal stronger, but this is a mixture, not a compound: the bonding is still metallic.

Alloying can also change other properties. It can improve corrosion resistance (stainless steel), lower the melting point (solder), change the colour (rose gold, brass), or lower the cost.

Steels and gold alloys

AlloyMain componentsUseful propertyUse
Steel (mild)Fe + about 0.1–0.3 % CStrong, easily pressed into shapeCar bodies, construction
Tool steel / high-carbon steelFe + more C (+ W, Mo, V)Very hard, keeps hardness when hotDrill bits, cutting tools
Stainless steelFe + about 18 % Cr + 8 % NiCorrosion resistantCutlery, surgical instruments, sinks
BrassCu + ZnHarder than Cu, gold coloured, does not corrode easilyMusical instruments, door fittings
BronzeCu + SnHard, corrosion resistantStatues, medals, ship propellers
PewterSn + Sb/CuLow melting point, easy to castDecorative ware
Gold alloys (9 ct, 18 ct, rose gold)Au + Cu/AgHarder and cheaper than pure gold; still unreactiveJewellery
DuraluminAl + Cu + MgLow density but much stronger than AlAircraft parts

Gold purity is measured in carats: pure gold is 24 carat, so the percentage of gold = (carat value ÷ 24) × 100.

What is the percentage of gold in 12 carat gold?

Pure gold is 24 carat. 12/24 × 100 = 50 %.

Use the chart: what is the percentage of silver in 18 carat gold?

Gold reaches 75 % and silver takes the bar up to 80 %, so silver is 80 − 75 = 5 %. (Check: 18/24 × 100 = 75 % gold.)
Suggest two reasons why 9 carat gold is often used instead of pure gold to make jewellery
  • Cost: 9 carat gold is cheaper (only 37.5 % gold).
  • Pure (24 carat) gold is soft; the alloy is harder and stronger, so it keeps its shape and resists scratching.
  • The other metals can change the colour (e.g. rose gold has more copper).
Exam tip"Why is jewellery made from a gold alloy rather than pure gold?" Pure gold is too soft (malleable) and expensive. Adding Cu or Ag makes it harder and cheaper, and gold stays unreactive so the jewellery does not corrode. "Explain why iron can form alloys with other transition metals." The atoms have similar radii (and electronegativities), and metallic bonding is non-directional, so the different atoms can take places in the same lattice.
Exam question [2]: Stainless steel contains about 18 % chromium and 8 % nickel. Explain why iron can form alloys with other transition metals. Answer, then reveal the markscheme
  • Their atoms/ions have similar (only slightly different) radii, densities and properties ✓
  • so they do not disrupt the crystal structure/metallic lattice significantly ✓

The examiners reported that this was very poorly answered: most candidates gave a general explanation of how alloys form instead of focusing on the similar sizes of transition-metal atoms.

Exam question: (a) explain how electricity is conducted in a metal, describing its structure and bonding [4]; (b) describe how the structure of an alloy differs from a pure metal [2]

(a) Giant structure/lattice of close-packed layers ✓; made of positive ions ✓; with delocalized electrons ✓; the electrons can move through the metal and carry charge ✓.

(b) An alloy contains different types/sizes of atoms ✓; so the layers are distorted and unable to slide as easily ✓. Do not call an alloy a compound.

Common mistakeAn alloy is a mixture, not a compound. Its composition can vary and no new chemical bonds of a different type form. The bonding is still metallic.

title: Polymers and addition polymerization
html:
S2.4.4 Polymers

Do now: if two ethene molecules are to join together, what would need to happen, and why? Try drawing a molecule made of two ethenes joined together.

Mono = one, poly = many, mer = part. A polymer is a very large molecule (macromolecule; macro = large) made of many repeating units joined by covalent bonds. The small molecules that join together are monomers. Not every molecule can be a monomer: water is a molecule but not a monomer, while ethene can join to itself to form long chains.

  • Natural polymers include starch, cellulose, proteins and DNA.
  • Synthetic polymers (plastics) include poly(ethene), PVC, PTFE, nylon and PET.

The properties of a polymer depend on the monomer(s), the type of linkage, the chain length, branching and the strength of the intermolecular forces between chains. Physical properties can also be varied by changing the reaction conditions (pressure, temperature, catalyst), which change chain length and branching. Plastics are useful because they are light, strong, easily moulded, electrical and thermal insulators, and chemically unreactive. That same inertness makes most of them non-biodegradable, so they persist in the environment and cause pollution.

S2.4.5 Addition polymers

Addition polymers form from monomers that contain a C=C double bond (alkenes and their derivatives). In addition polymerization, the π bond of each C=C breaks and the monomers join end to end through new C–C single bonds, forming a long saturated chain.

  1. Step 1: break the double bond (the π bond) in each ethene.
  2. Step 2: join the molecules together through new C–C bonds. The product is poly(ethene) and the process is polymerization.
n CH₂=CH₂ → –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– (ethene → poly(ethene))
General: n CH₂=CHX → –[CH₂–CHX]ₙ–
  • All the atoms of the monomer end up in the polymer. There is only one product and no by-product, so the atom economy is 100 %.
  • The repeating unit is drawn in square brackets with continuation bonds passing through the brackets, and n outside. n represents a large number.
  • Industrially, addition polymers are often made by a free-radical process at high pressure and temperature with an initiator (e.g. a peroxide), which breaks up into radicals that start a chain reaction.

Which molecule can act as a monomer for addition polymerization?

  1. Ethane, C₂H₆
  2. Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl
  3. Water, H₂O
  4. Ethanol, C₂H₅OH

Addition polymerization needs a C=C double bond. Chloroethene has one and gives PVC. Ethane, water and ethanol are saturated.

MonomerPolymerRepeating unitUses
Ethene, CH₂=CH₂Poly(ethene), PE–[CH₂–CH₂]–Plastic bags, bottles, film
Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃Poly(propene), PP–[CH₂–CH(CH₃)]–Crates, ropes, food containers
Chloroethene, CH₂=CHClPoly(chloroethene), PVC–[CH₂–CHCl]–Pipes, window frames, cable insulation
Tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂Poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE–[CF₂–CF₂]–Non-stick coatings
Phenylethene (styrene), CH₂=CHC₆H₅Poly(phenylethene), PS–[CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)]–Packaging, insulation

Going from monomer to repeating unit, and back

  1. Draw the monomer with the C=C in the middle and the four substituents above and below.
  2. Change C=C to C–C, keep all the substituents, and add a continuation bond on each side.
  3. To go backwards, take a two-carbon section of the main chain, remove the continuation bonds and put a C=C between the two carbons.
Worked example

Question: An addition polymer has the repeating unit –[CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)]–. Identify the monomer.

Both main-chain carbons carry an H and a CH₃. Put the double bond between them: CH₃CH=CHCH₃, but-2-ene. (Note: but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, would give –[CH₂–CH(C₂H₅)]– instead.)

Worked example

Question: Draw a section of poly(propene) showing two repeating units.

–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–

The CH₃ groups are branches on alternate carbons. They are not part of the main chain. Show continuation bonds at both ends.

Exam question: (a) draw 2-methylpropene and the repeating unit of poly(2-methylpropene); (b) deduce the atom economy of the polymerization. Then reveal

(a) Monomer: H₂C=C(CH₃)₂. Repeating unit: –[CH₂–C(CH₃)₂]– with continuation bonds.

(b) 100 %: the polymer has the same total mass as the monomer used, as no other product forms.

Common mistakeStudents often put the CH₃ of propene into the main chain (writing –CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–). Only the two C=C carbons form the backbone. Another error is leaving a C=C in the polymer: the polymer chain is saturated.

Which is the repeating unit of PTFE?

  1. –[CF₂=CF₂]–
  2. –[CH₂–CF₂]–
  3. –[CF₂–CF₂]–
  4. –[CF₂]–

The monomer CF₂=CF₂ loses its double bond, so the repeating unit is –[CF₂–CF₂]–. A repeating unit for an addition polymer always contains the two carbons from the C=C.

Summary: addition polymers are made from alkene monomers; the C=C breaks to form a –C–C– linkage, joining unsaturated molecules into a long saturated molecule; only one product forms; and the product is unreactive (inert), which explains both its usefulness and its persistence as waste.

title: Condensation polymers (AHL)
html:
S2.4.6 Condensation polymers AHL

Do now: write down everything you know about polymers already. How might condensation polymers differ from addition ones?

DefinitionA condensation reaction is one in which two molecules join to form a larger molecule, with the elimination of a small molecule such as water (or HCl). Condensation polymerization repeats this many times between monomers that each have two functional groups (bifunctional monomers).
Addition polymerizationCondensation polymerization
Monomer requirementC=C double bondTwo reactive functional groups per monomer (e.g. –OH, –COOH, –NH₂, –COCl)
By-productNone (one product only)Small molecule (H₂O or HCl) for each link formed
LinkageC–CEster (–COO–) or amide (–CONH–) etc.
ExamplesPE, PP, PVC, PTFEPolyesters (PET), polyamides (nylon, Kevlar®, proteins), polysaccharides
Can be hydrolysed?No (C–C backbone is very inert)Yes: the linkage can be split by water/acid/enzymes
Exam question [1]: describe how the monomers of addition polymers and of condensation polymers differ

Addition: monomers contain a C=C (double/multiple bond) ✓ AND condensation: two functional groups are needed on each monomer.

Polyesters AHL

Polyesters form from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, or from a single hydroxycarboxylic acid that has both groups. Each –OH reacts with a –COOH to form an ester linkage –COO– and eliminate H₂O.

n HO–CH₂CH₂–OH + n HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH → –[O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO]ₙ– + 2n H₂O

This is PET (polyethylene terephthalate, Terylene), made from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, and used for drinks bottles and polyester fibres. Poly(lactic acid), PLA, is a polyester made from the hydroxycarboxylic acid 2-hydroxypropanoic (lactic) acid. It is biodegradable.

Draw the repeating unit of the polyester formed from (a) ethanediol and propanedioic acid, (b) methanediol and butanedioic acid. Then reveal

(a) –[O–CH₂–CH₂–O–CO–CH₂–CO]–

(b) –[O–CH₂–O–CO–CH₂–CH₂–CO]–

In each, the diol part keeps its O atoms and the acid part keeps its two C=O groups; one H₂O is lost per ester link.

Exam question: on gentle heating, 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid forms a cyclic compound T (C₆H₁₀O₂); under other conditions it forms a polyester. Draw T and the repeating unit, and name the type of polymerization

T is a six-membered ring ester (lactone): the –OH on C5 reacts with the –COOH on the same molecule, losing H₂O.

Repeating unit: –[O–CH(CH₃)–(CH₂)₃–CO]– (with trailing bonds). Type: condensation polymerization.

Polyamides AHL

Polyamides form from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid (or a diacyl chloride), or from a single monomer with both an –NH₂ and a –COOH group (an amino acid). The –NH₂ reacts with –COOH to form an amide linkage –CONH– and eliminate H₂O. With an acyl chloride, –COCl, the by-product is HCl.

n H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂ + n HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH → –[NH–(CH₂)₆–NH–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO]ₙ– + 2n H₂O (nylon-6,6)
  • Kevlar®: repeating unit –[CO–C₆H₄–CO–NH–C₆H₄–NH]–, made from benzene-1,4-diamine (H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂) and benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl chloride (ClOC–C₆H₄–COCl), eliminating HCl. Its rigid, straight chains are held together by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups on neighbouring chains, making it extremely strong (bullet-proof vests).

Which compound can form a polymer without needing another reagent?

  1. HOCH₂CH₂OH
  2. HOOCCH₂CH₂COOH
  3. HOCH₂CH₂COCl
  4. ClCH₂CH₂COOH

HOCH₂CH₂COCl has an –OH at one end and an acyl chloride at the other, so molecules can join head to tail forming ester links (eliminating HCl). A diol or a diacid alone needs a partner; ClCH₂CH₂COOH has no group that forms an ester or amide link with –COOH.

Proteins: natural polyamides AHL

Proteins are natural polyamides (polypeptides). Amino acids (H₂N–CHR–COOH, which differ only in the R group) join through amide linkages, called peptide bonds in biochemistry. Two amino acids give a dipeptide plus one H₂O.

Worked example

Question: Deduce the repeating unit of the polymer formed from glycine (H₂N–CH₂–COOH) alone, and state the by-product.

  1. The –NH₂ of one glycine reacts with the –COOH of the next: –COOH + H₂N– → –CO–NH– + H₂O.
  2. Repeating unit: –[NH–CH₂–CO]–
  3. By-product: water (one molecule per amide linkage).
Task: draw the tripeptide made from glycine, alanine and glycine (in that order). Then reveal

H₂N–CH₂–CO–NH–CH(CH₃)–CO–NH–CH₂–COOH

Two amide linkages, two molecules of water eliminated. The free –NH₂ is at the glycine end on the left and the free –COOH at the glycine end on the right.

How many water molecules are eliminated when three glycine molecules join to form a tripeptide?

Number of links = number of monomers − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2, and each amide link releases one H₂O.

Polysaccharides AHL

Glucose (a monosaccharide; saccharide means sugar) is the monomer for starch and cellulose (plant cell walls), which are polysaccharides. Glucose molecules link through condensation between two –OH groups, forming a C–O–C glycosidic (ether) linkage and eliminating water. Starch is therefore a condensation polymer.

Hydrolysis AHL

Condensation polymers can be broken back into their monomers by hydrolysis (adding water across the linkage; "splitting with water"), which is the reverse of condensation. It is catalysed by acid, alkali or enzymes. Digestion hydrolyses proteins into amino acids and starch into glucose. Because ester and amide linkages can be hydrolysed, some condensation polymers (e.g. PLA) are more biodegradable than addition polymers.

Exam question: the polymer of ethyl 2-methylpropenoate, H₂C=C(CH₃)COOCH₂CH₃, and the polyester of 5-hydroxyhexanoic acid both contain ester groups. Explain why only the polyester is biodegradable

In poly(ethyl 2-methylpropenoate) the main chain is made of strong, non-polar C–C bonds, which cannot be attacked by nucleophiles/acids, i.e. cannot be hydrolysed ✓. The ester group is only in the side chain, so hydrolysing it does not break the chain ✓. In the polyester, the polar ester links are in the main chain and can be hydrolysed, breaking the polymer down.

Worked example

Question: Deduce the monomers of the polymer with repeating unit –[O–(CH₂)₂–O–CO–(CH₂)₄–CO]–.

  1. Identify the linkage: –O–CO– is an ester.
  2. Split each ester at the C–O bond between the carbonyl carbon and the oxygen. Add –OH to each C=O end, and add H to each O end.
  3. Monomers: HO–(CH₂)₂–OH (ethane-1,2-diol) and HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH (hexanedioic acid).
Exam tipWhen asked for monomers from a polyamide, split at the C–N bond of each –CO–NH–: give the C=O end an –OH (or –Cl if the question says HCl is produced) and the N end an extra H. Always check the by-product stated in the question.
Common mistakeDrawing an ester or amide linkage the wrong way round, or forgetting that the by-product count is one small molecule per linkage (2n H₂O for n diol + n diacid). Also, condensation polymers do not need a C=C.

Which polymer, A–E, represents a protein?

  1. A
  2. B
  3. E
  4. D

D contains –NH–CO– amide linkages with different units (different R groups) between them: a polypeptide. E is an addition polymer (poly(propene)), B is a polyester from one monomer, C is a polyester from two monomers (like Terylene), and A, with C–O–C links, represents a complex carbohydrate.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • "Use the bonding triangle to deduce the bonding in X." Show both calculations (Δχ and average), state the coordinates, then name the region.
  • "Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals." [2] Atoms of different sizes distort the regular lattice ✓, so layers cannot slide over one another as easily ✓.
  • "Draw two repeating units of the polymer from propene." [1] –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH(CH₃)– with continuation bonds.
  • AHL "State the type of polymerization and the other product." Condensation; H₂O (or HCl if an acyl chloride is used).
  • AHL "Deduce the monomers of Kevlar®/nylon/PET." Split at each linkage and restore –OH/–Cl and –H.
